column3: Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats “name” for both wives and explicitly repeats “children” for Hannah’s lack of them.
The Hebrew begins with “that man” rather than repeating Elkanah.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew explicitly repeats Hannah’s name and joins the LORD’s closing her womb with “and”; BSB uses “her” and “even though.”
The Hebrew identifies her only with pronouns, rather than explicitly repeating Hannah.
The Hebrew begins with an active masculine singular “he did so”; BSB uses the impersonal “this went on.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew separately mentions eating and drinking without an explicit plural subject; BSB supplies “they.”
The Hebrew names bitterness of soul and intensifies the weeping by repeating its root; BSB has “bitter distress” and “many tears.”
The Hebrew repeats the vow root in verb and noun and describes a male child as “seed of men.”
The Hebrew leaves Hannah unnamed, while BSB repeats her name.
The Hebrew says Hannah was “speaking”; BSB interprets this as praying.
The Hebrew explicitly names Eli as speaker.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew calls a worthless woman a “daughter of worthlessness” and says “I have spoken”; BSB has “wicked woman” and “have been praying.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed, then names “the woman,” and says simply that she ate; BSB names Hannah, then uses “she,” and adds beginning to eat again.
The Hebrew leaves the early risers unnamed and says Elkanah “knew” Hannah; BSB supplies their names and interprets knowing as having relations.
The Hebrew describes the passage of time as a cycle of days.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew says the boy will “appear” and explicitly names the LORD’s “face”; BSB has taking him “to appear before the LORD.”
The Hebrew says “good in your eyes” and later names “the woman”; BSB has “what you think is best” and names Hannah.
The Hebrew has “three bulls,” whereas BSB has “a three-year-old bull.” It repeats the word “boy” in describing his youth.
The Hebrew coordinates slaughtering and bringing with “and”; BSB makes slaughtering a “when” clause.
The Hebrew leaves the speaker unnamed and uses “your soul lives”; BSB names Hannah and says “you live.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew repeats a lending or entrusting root and ends with a singular masculine worshipper; BSB uses “dedicate” and plural “they worshiped.”
